title: Iran's Hormuz Toll Authority Says 300 Ships Have Applied for Safe Passage. Most Want to Reach India and China.
excerpt: The Persian Gulf Strait Authority, now under US sanctions, says 77% of applicants are oil tankers heading to Asia — but Washington has told vessels not to pay.
body:
At least 300 non-Iranian ships have applied for permission to transit the Strait of Hormuz through Tehran's newly created toll authority, Iran announced on Tuesday — a move that lays bare the Islamic Republic's effort to turn the world's most critical oil chokepoint into a permanent revenue stream.

The Persian Gulf Strait Authority (PGSA), established by Iran after the February 28 conflict began, said the majority of applicants were oil tankers. Seventy-seven per cent of them sought to exit the Persian Gulf and reach Asia, with India and China — the Middle East's two largest crude buyers — as the primary destinations.

## A Toll Booth Over Global Energy

The PGSA said it would not issue permits to ships from "hostile countries," a designation Tehran applies to the United States and Israel. It did not disclose how much each vessel would be charged, though earlier reports suggested oil tankers could pay as much as $2 million per transit.

The announcement drew a sharp response from Washington. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent sanctioned the PGSA last week, calling it an extortion scheme. "The Iranian military's latest attempt to extort global maritime trade is proof that Economic Fury has left the regime desperate for cash," Bessent said. He warned that anyone providing money to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) would face US sanctions.

The United States has explicitly instructed all commercial vessels not to pay Iran's transit fees.

## 24 Vessels in 24 Hours

The IRGC said its naval forces escorted 24 vessels through the strait over the past 24 hours. Separately, US Central Command (CENTCOM) has said approximately 70 commercial ships have transited the strait in the past three weeks — many by turning off their transponders and receiving CENTCOM guidance to avoid Iranian mines and drones.

The two competing claims illustrate the surreal dual-authority situation at Hormuz, where American and Iranian naval forces are both claiming to facilitate — and police — the same waterway.

## What It Means for India

India is among the countries most exposed to the Hormuz disruption. Before the conflict, roughly 60% of India's crude imports transited the strait. While New Delhi has aggressively diversified — turning to Venezuela, Africa, and the Americas — the loss of easy Gulf access has driven up freight rates, insurance premiums, and the price of every barrel India buys.

Goldman Sachs last week named India the most vulnerable major economy to the Hormuz closure, estimating a potential GDP hit of 3.6%. The PGSA's toll scheme adds a new layer of uncertainty for Indian refiners already navigating a fractured supply chain.

For Indian consumers, the downstream effects are tangible: higher petrol prices, rising cooking gas costs, and a weakening rupee. Whether New Delhi engages with the PGSA or continues to route cargoes through alternative pipelines will be one of the defining trade decisions of the year.

The strait, which carried about a fifth of the world's daily crude supply before the war, remains effectively closed for most commercial traffic 94 days into the conflict.
author: Diaspora Desk
